newsitem.title: USA: US nurses to strike at Kaiser Permanente hospitals.
newsitem.headline: US nurses to strike at Kaiser Permanente hospitals.

text.p: Some 7,500 nurses employed by Kaiser Permanente, the nation's largest health maintenance organization, will walk off the job for one day Wednesday over proposed pay cuts and staff reductions.
The nurses may be joined by as many as 26,000 other healthcare workers, housekeepers and clerical workers of the HMO who the nurses' union said have supported their proposed job action.

The strike, expected to last 24 hours, is being organized by the California Nurses Association's northern California unit, which is seeking to have provisions addressing the quality of patient care written into a new labor contract. The strike will cover 16 Kaiser Permanente hospitals and 29 clinics.

"Nurses feel they are unable to give the quality of care Kaiser has historically guaranteed its patients," Carl Bloice, a spokesman for the Nurses Association, whose labor contract expired in January, said.

"They are overworked, and their responsibilities are being farmed out to less-qualified workers," he added, citing a 15 percent drop in the number of nurses employed by Kaiser over the past three years.

Kaiser, which is moving some southern California employees up to the San Francisco area for the day and will have staff doctors fill in as nurses, said the union's claim that it wants to cut their salaries is exaggerated.

A spokesman for Kaiser said it had proposed 2.5 percent annual pay cuts over the next six years for 60 percent of its nurses in a bid to bring salaries in line with the industry norm. The average registered nurse at Kaiser currently earns $62,000 a year, he said.

Kaiser is also denying charges it has cut jobs to save money and said the drop in the number of nurses corresponds to a larger drop in its patient load, resulting from more outpatient and in-home procedures.

While the charges facing Kaiser echo complaints being made against HMO's around the country, many critics say the erosion in patient care has been especially acute in California, one of the nation's most competitive HMO markets.
